overview: This bill, the Taiwan Allies Fund Act, would set aside up to $10 million a year for fiscal years 2026 through 2028, from an existing State Department fund for countering China's influence, to help countries that stand by Taiwan. The money could go to countries that have official ties with Taiwan, or have meaningfully strengthened unofficial ties, and that have faced pressure from China because of it but lack the means to resist on their own. It could pay for things like alternatives to Chinese-backed health, digital, energy, and development projects, support for local media and civil society, moving supply chains away from China, and helping Taiwan take part in international organizations. No single country could get more than $5 million a year, the State Department would be urged to share costs with Taiwan, and it would report yearly to Congress on results. As of February 10, 2026, the Senate Foreign Relations Committee had approved it and it was awaiting a vote by the full Senate.
for: Supporters say modest, targeted aid can help small countries withstand Chinese pressure to cut ties with Taiwan, supporting a democratic partner and U.S. interests at low cost.
against: Critics say tying foreign aid to countries' stance on Taiwan could heighten tensions with China, and that the program's results in shaping other nations' diplomatic choices may be hard to measure.
